structural_memory.memory: Cargo-tank inert-gas service spans owner/manager, master and deck/cargo team, engineering crew, shore technical or cargo support, inert-gas equipment/service actors and relevant terminal, port or yard support. Cargo-operation context, machinery support, tank-scope assurance, monitoring and shore intervention should remain distinct roles rather than one vendor, gas-testing, tanker-operation or safety-procedure directory.

Inert-gas source or generation readiness is distinct from downstream supply/distribution availability. A source can be ready while the delivery path to a bounded tank scope is unavailable, and a distribution concern does not itself prove source failure.

Gas-condition or quality confidence is distinct from source/generation readiness. Apparent source operation does not by itself establish suitable delivered gas condition, while a condition concern does not identify the exact source, treatment or measurement cause.

Supply/distribution availability is distinct from tank-interface or tank-scope confidence. A common distribution path can be available while a particular tank connection or bounded tank scope remains unavailable or uncertain.

Cargo-tank scope must remain explicit: inert-gas service confidence can differ by tank, tank group, manifolded branch or other bounded cargo-tank scope. A localized concern should not be generalized to all cargo tanks without exact arrangement evidence.

Pressure or gas-blanket confidence can be represented structurally without numeric pressure values or operating limits. The useful memory distinction is confidence, uncertainty, restriction and verified restoration; no setpoint or adjustment guidance is retained.

Monitoring/alarm confidence is distinct from the physical gas-condition and pressure/blanket state. Indication or alarm status can alter confidence but does not alone establish exact composition, pressure, duration, root cause or corrective action.

Support-dependency confidence is a separate dimension: electrical power, controls, cooling/water or other supporting services may enable inert-gas equipment, but their availability is not proof of delivered inert-gas service and their degradation is not automatically the root cause of an inert-gas outcome.

Multiple sources, paths or bounded tank scopes can create redundancy or substitution confidence, but structural memory should not infer exact approved alignments, source selection, valve arrangements, capacity or operating methods.

Inert-gas service degradation follows a defensive lifecycle: observation, uncertain source/gas-condition/distribution/tank-scope/blanket/monitoring scope, affected-state identification, restriction or uncertainty, bounded isolation, restoration indication and post-restoration verification. No purging, inerting, gas-testing, entry, cargo-operation or emergency procedure is retained.

Restriction or isolation should be scoped to the affected source, gas-condition domain, distribution branch, tank interface/scope or monitoring domain rather than generalized to the entire tanker cargo system. Exact valve actions, alignments and corrective steps remain deferred.

Inert-gas degradation can propagate into cargo-operation availability, cargo-condition or safety confidence, terminal compatibility, port rework or schedule, but those downstream effects are not by themselves proof of a source, gas-condition, distribution, tank-interface, pressure/blanket or monitoring root cause.

Restoration can have multiple timestamps: source/generation readiness returns, gas-condition confidence is re-established, distribution/tank-scope availability returns, non-numeric pressure/blanket confidence is renewed and monitoring confidence is restored. One running indication or alarm reset does not prove full inert-gas-service restoration.

P089 cargo-space ventilation concerns air exchange, while P091 cargo-tank inert-gas service concerns maintaining a bounded cargo-tank gas/blanket confidence state. Shared fan, gas or atmosphere vocabulary must not collapse ventilation and inerting into one service.

P090 refrigerated-cargo service maintains unit/cargo condition through power and interfaces, while P091 concerns tanker cargo-tank gas/blanket service. Both influence cargo-operation confidence but their physical paths and failure domains remain distinct.
P070 electrical service and P068 digital/control service are upstream support dimensions for inert-gas equipment and monitoring; neither equals delivered gas-condition or tank-blanket confidence.

Generic service-condition monitoring refines inert-gas confidence only at an epistemic level: observed indicators can change confidence without establishing exact gas composition, pressure adequacy, approved operating state or required action.
Generic source/distribution/support dependency, monitoring and restoration mechanics overlap prior shipboard utility and equipment-service passes.

Scoped degradation, restriction/isolation, downstream-effect separation and multi-stage restoration mechanics overlap prior shipboard service passes; P091 applies them specifically to cargo-tank inert-gas service.

It is not tanker operation, inerting/purging, gas-testing, tank-entry, cargo-handling, safety, emergency-response or vessel-operating advice and does not establish any exact arrangement, capacity, pressure, flow, oxygen/gas-quality value, valve position, tank connection, control mode, alarm threshold, test result, procedure, provider, incident, deficiency finding or current-readiness fact.
stop_reason: Cargo-tank inert-gas service is recalled at useful non-operational resolution: source/generation readiness, gas-condition confidence, supply/distribution availability, tank scope, non-numeric pressure/blanket confidence, monitoring/alarm confidence, support dependencies, scoped restriction/isolation and verified restoration are separable states. Further detail would become vessel-, tanker-type-, source-, pressure-, flow-, gas-quality-, valve-, tank-, test-, procedure-, provider- or incident-specific and is deferred to claim-scoped Evidence.
